name: Feedback Students Actually Use
title: Feedback Students Actually Use
answer: Feedback students actually use means tying AI writing feedback to the class rubric and making revision a required part of the assignment, so that students submit a draft, get feedback on specific rubric points, revise, and explain their changes. It matters because feedback that students never act on does nothing, and studies show many students ignore AI feedback entirely. The teacher still reads the final version and assigns the grade.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: Writing feedback is one of the strongest uses of AI in this volume, but the value depends on whether students do anything with it. The problem is that good feedback can sit unused: across more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12, nearly half did not change a single character after receiving AI feedback. The design that solves this ties feedback to the class rubric and builds revision into the assignment itself. A student submits a draft, receives feedback on specific rubric points, revises, and explains what they changed. The teacher then reads the final version and assigns the grade, so the feedback serves the rubric rather than floating free of it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, the cycle runs from draft to rubric-linked feedback to revision to a short explanation of what the student changed, with the teacher reading the final version and assigning the grade. Figure 6.3 shows this cycle. The text does not separate practice by grade band, though the caution about unused feedback comes from grades 1 through 12, and the trials it cites involve tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language. Teachers can also see who actually revised by checking Google Docs version history, which shows every change a student made and when. Tracking this for a few weeks often surprises teachers and gives them a clear, fair basis for conversations with students who are not revising.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research evidence. In a randomized trial with 459 tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language, feedback from an AI model improved the quality of their revisions and raised their motivation for future writing (Meyer et al., 2023). A later trial found no clear difference in revision quality between teacher feedback and AI feedback, though teacher feedback may have carried over slightly better to the next task (Meyer et al., 2026). A review of 20 studies found a medium effect of automated writing feedback overall (Fleckenstein et al., 2023). Two cautions sit alongside these findings: when researchers compared feedback side by side, trained teachers still wrote better feedback than an AI in most categories (Steiss et al., 2024), and across more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12, nearly half did not change a single character after receiving AI feedback (Jansen et al., 2025).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that feedback which is not acted on does nothing, however good it is, and the evidence shows this happens at scale. AI feedback also does not match trained teachers, who still wrote better feedback than an AI in most categories when compared side by side. The decisions that stay with a person are the rubric itself, the requirement that revision be part of the assignment, and the final grade, which the teacher assigns after reading the final version. Teachers can use Google Docs version history to see whether feedback led to real revision or none at all, which supports fair conversations with students who are not revising. The text does not set out further legal or policy limits, so these are practice decisions rather than compliance rules.
